plain_english: A reasonable soul has natural powers and privileges. It can see itself clearly. It can order and shape itself. It makes itself into what it chooses to be. And it enjoys its own fruits, whatever they may be. Plants, trees, and unreasoning creatures bear their fruit for others, not for themselves.
original_excerpt: The natural properties, and privileges of a reasonable soul are: That she seeth herself; that she can order, and compose herself: that she makes herself as she will herself: that she reaps her own fruits whatsoever, whereas plants, trees, unreasonable creatures, what fruit soever (be it either fruit properly, or analogically only) they bear, they bear them unto others, and not to themselves.

plain_english: Whenever and wherever her life ends, sooner or later, she has her own complete ending. She is not like dancers or actors who, if interrupted in the middle of their performance, leave their work unfinished. Nature can be stopped at any moment and still make whatever she has in hand complete and whole. She can depart with this comfort: 'I have lived. I lack nothing that properly belonged to me.'
original_excerpt: Again; whensoever, and wheresoever, sooner or later, her life doth end, she hath her own end nevertheless. For it is not with her, as with dancers and players, who if they be interrupted in any part of their action, the whole action must needs be imperfect: but she in what part of time or action soever she be surprised, can make that which she hath in her hand whatsoever it be, complete and full, so that she may depart with that comfort, 'I have lived; neither want I anything of that which properly did belong unto me.'

plain_english: The mind takes in the whole world. It sees through the emptiness and surface appearance of things. It reaches toward endless time. It grasps how all things return to the same place after certain periods. It understands this clearly: those who come after us will see nothing new that we have not seen. Those who came before saw nothing more than we do. Anyone who reaches forty years old, if they have any sense at all, can see all things — past and future. Everything follows the same patterns.
original_excerpt: Again, she compasseth the whole world, and penetrateth into the vanity, and mere outside (wanting substance and solidity) of it, and stretcheth herself unto the infiniteness of eternity; and the revolution or restoration of all things after a certain period of time, to the same state and place as before, she fetcheth about, and doth comprehend in herself; and considers withal, and sees clearly this, that neither they that shall follow us, shall see any new thing, that we have not seen, nor they that went before, anything more than we: but that he that is once come to forty (if he have any wit at all) can in a manner (for that they are all of one kind) see all things, both past and future.

plain_english: It is natural for the human soul to love others, to be honest and humble, and to value nothing more than itself. This is also the nature of law. This shows that sound reason and justice are the same thing. Therefore justice is the main goal that thinking beings should set for themselves.
original_excerpt: As proper is it, and natural to the soul of man to love her neighbour, to be true and modest; and to regard nothing so much as herself: which is also the property of the law: whereby by the way it appears, that sound reason and justice comes all to one, and therefore that justice is the chief thing, that reasonable creatures ought to propose unto themselves as their end.

plain_english: A beautiful song or dance, athletic contests — things that normally captivate you — you can easily dismiss if you break them down. Take a lovely voice and split it into each separate sound it's made of. Ask yourself about each one: is this particular sound what overpowers me? You'll feel foolish. Do the same with dance — examine each movement and pose by itself. Same with wrestling matches. In general, whatever grabs your attention (except virtue and what flows from virtue), immediately break it apart like this. When you divide it up, you'll find yourself looking down on the whole thing. Apply this method to your entire life.
original_excerpt: A pleasant song or dance; the Pancratiast's exercise, sports that thou art wont to be much taken with, thou shalt easily contemn; if the harmonious voice thou shalt divide into so many particular sounds whereof it doth consist, and of every one in particular shall ask thyself; whether this or that sound is it, that doth so conquer thee. For thou wilt be ashamed of it. And so for shame, if accordingly thou shalt consider it, every particular motion and posture by itself: and so for the wrestler's exercise too. Generally then, whatsoever it be, besides virtue, and those things that proceed from virtue that thou art subject to be much affected with, remember presently thus to divide it, and by this kind of division, in each particular to attain unto the contempt of the whole. This thou must transfer and apply to thy whole life also.

plain_english: How blessed is the soul that is always ready to leave the body — whether that means going out of existence, scattering, or continuing somewhere else. But this readiness must not come from stubborn defiance or violent passion, like we see in Christians. It should come from careful thought and quiet dignity. This way others might be convinced to follow the same path, without drama or emotional outbursts.
original_excerpt: That soul which is ever ready, even now presently (if need be) from the body, whether by way of extinction, or dispersion, or continuation in another place and estate to be separated, how blessed and happy is it! But this readiness of it, it must proceed, not from an obstinate and peremptory resolution of the mind, violently and passionately set upon Opposition, as Christians are wont; but from a peculiar judgment; with discretion and gravity, so that others may be persuaded also and drawn to the like example, but without any noise and passionate exclamations.

plain_english: Have I done something kind? Then I have gained from it. Keep this thought always in mind. Never stop thinking about it. What is your job? To be good. And how can you do this well? Only by understanding certain principles. Some about how the universe works, and some about what makes humans who they are.
original_excerpt: Have I done anything charitably? then am I benefited by it. See that this upon all occasions may present itself unto thy mind, and never cease to think of it. What is thy profession? to be good. And how should this be well brought to pass, but by certain theorems and doctrines; some Concerning the nature of the universe, and some Concerning the proper and particular constitution of man?

plain_english: Tragedies were first created to remind people of life's twists and turns. These things happen naturally. People who enjoy watching disasters on stage shouldn't be surprised when the same things happen to them in real life on a bigger scale. You can see how these stories end. Even the characters who cry out in grief to the mountains must bear their suffering, just like everyone else. These poets actually say many wise things. For example: "If the gods neglect me and my two children, they must have their reasons." And: "It does no good to rage against what happens to you." And: "A life should be harvested like ripe grain." There are many other lines like these.
original_excerpt: Tragedies were at first brought in and instituted, to put men in mind of worldly chances and casualties: that these things in the ordinary course of nature did so happen: that men that were much pleased and delighted by such accidents upon this stage, would not by the same things in a greater stage be grieved and afflicted: for here you see what is the end of all such things; and that even they that cry out so mournfully to Cithaeron, must bear them for all their cries and exclamations, as well as others. And in very truth many good things are spoken by these poets; as that (for example) is an excellent passage: 'But if so be that I and my two children be neglected by the Gods, they have some reason even for that,' &c. And again, 'It will but little avail thee to storm and rage against the things themselves,' &c. Again, 'To reap one's life, as a ripe ear of corn;' and whatsoever else is to be found in them, that is of the same kind.

plain_english: After tragedy came ancient comedy, which had the freedom to attack personal flaws. This freedom of speech was useful—it kept people from becoming proud and arrogant. Diogenes used this same freedom too. But what about Middle Comedy and New Comedy? They were allowed mostly just for entertainment and clever acting. They might say things like 'It will steal away; look to it,' and so on. Sure, these plays had some good points. But what was the real purpose of this whole type of drama? Just what I said—entertainment.
original_excerpt: After the tragedy, the ancient comedy was brought in, which had the liberty to inveigh against personal vices; being therefore through this her freedom and liberty of speech of very good use and effect, to restrain men from pride and arrogancy. To which end it was, that Diogenes took also the same liberty. After these, what were either the Middle, or New Comedy admitted for, but merely, (Or for the most part at least) for the delight and pleasure of curious and excellent imitation? 'It will steal away; look to it,' &c. Why, no man denies, but that these also have some good things whereof that may be one: but the whole drift and foundation of that kind of dramatical poetry, what is it else, but as we have said?

plain_english: How clearly you can see that no other way of living would suit a true philosopher better than the life you are living right now.
original_excerpt: How clearly doth it appear unto thee, that no other course of thy life could fit a true philosopher's practice better, than this very course, that thou art now already in?

plain_english:
A branch cut off from the tree it was attached to must be cut off from the whole tree. In the same way, a person who separates himself from another person separates himself from all of society. Someone else cuts off a branch. But when you hate someone and turn away from them, you cut yourself off from your neighbor. You don't realize that you're also cutting yourself off from the whole community.

But here is God's gift and mercy — he made this society so that once we're cut off, we can grow back together and become part of the whole again. But if this happens too often, the problem gets worse. The farther you go in this separation, the harder it becomes to reunite and heal again. Any gardener will tell you this: a branch that was cut off and then grafted back in is never quite like the one that grew naturally from the beginning and stayed connected to the tree.
original_excerpt: A branch cut off from the continuity of that which was next unto it, must needs be cut off from the whole tree: so a man that is divided from another man, is divided from the whole society. A branch is cut off by another, but he that hates and is averse, cuts himself off from his neighbour, and knows not that at the same time he divides himself from the whole body, or corporation. But herein is the gift and mercy of God, the Author of this society, in that, once cut off we may grow together and become part of the whole again. But if this happen often the misery is that the further a man is run in this division, the harder he is to be reunited and restored again: and however the branch which, once cut of afterwards was graffed in, gardeners can tell you is not like that which sprouted together at first, and still continued in the unity of the body.

plain_english: Grow close to others in friendship and care, but not in opinions. When people oppose your right actions, they can't force you to stop doing good. Don't let them make you stop caring about them either. Keep yourself steady in both things: right judgment and action, and true kindness toward those who try to block you or get upset with what you do. To fail at either one — giving up from fear, or abandoning your natural care for someone who is your friend and fellow human — is equally shameful. It's like being a coward who runs from battle.
original_excerpt: To grow together like fellow branches in matter of good correspondence and affection; but not in matter of opinions. They that shall oppose thee in thy right courses, as it is not in their power to divert thee from thy good action, so neither let it be to divert thee from thy good affection towards them. But be it thy care to keep thyself constant in both; both in a right judgment and action, and in true meekness towards them, that either shall do their endeavour to hinder thee, or at least will be displeased with thee for what thou hast done. For to fail in either (either in the one to give over for fear, or in the other to forsake thy natural affection towards him, who by nature is both thy friend and thy kinsman) is equally base, and much savouring of the disposition of a cowardly fugitive soldier.

plain_english: No nature can be inferior to art, since all arts copy nature. If this is true, then it's unlikely that the most perfect nature of all would fall short of what artists can do. All arts commonly make something worse for the sake of something better. The common nature does this even more. This is where justice begins. All other virtues come from justice. We cannot preserve justice if we fix our minds on worldly things, or if we are easily fooled, rash, or inconsistent.
original_excerpt: It is not possible that any nature should be inferior unto art, since that all arts imitate nature. If this be so; that the most perfect and general nature of all natures should in her operation come short of the skill of arts, is most improbable. Now common is it to all arts, to make that which is worse for the better's sake. Much more then doth the common nature do the same. Hence is the first ground of justice. From justice all other virtues have their existence. For justice cannot be preserved, if either we settle our minds and affections upon worldly things; or be apt to be deceived, or rash, and inconstant.

plain_english: The things that cause you so much trouble — the things you chase after or try to avoid — don't actually come to you. You go to them. Let your judgment about these things be at peace. The things themselves are still and quiet, making no noise at all. When you do this, all your chasing and running away will stop.
original_excerpt: The things themselves (which either to get or to avoid thou art put to so much trouble) come not unto thee themselves; but thou in a manner goest unto them. Let then thine own judgment and opinion concerning those things be at rest; and as for the things themselves, they stand still and quiet, without any noise or stir at all; and so shall all pursuing and flying cease.

plain_english: The soul is like a perfect sphere, as Empedocles said. It keeps its natural shape. It doesn't reach out greedily for things or shrink back in fear. It doesn't collapse or get depressed. Instead it shines with its own light. In that light, it sees the true nature of everything — both the universe and itself.
original_excerpt: Then is the soul as Empedocles doth liken it, like unto a sphere or globe, when she is all of one form and figure: when she neither greedily stretcheth out herself unto anything, nor basely contracts herself, or lies flat and dejected; but shineth all with light, whereby she does see and behold the true nature, both that of the universe, and her own in particular.

plain_english: Will someone look down on me? Let them worry about their reasons. My job is to make sure I never do or say anything that actually deserves contempt. Will someone hate me? That's their business. I'll be kind and loving to everyone, even to whoever hates me. I'll be ready to show them their mistake — not to prove how patient I am, but honestly and gently, like the famous Phocion did (if he wasn't just pretending). These things have to come from the inside. The gods see what's inside, not what shows on the surface. They want to see a person truly free from anger and pain. What harm can another person's actions do to you, as long as you can do what fits your nature? Won't you — someone meant to serve the common good — accept what the universe requires right now?
original_excerpt: Will any contemn me? let him look to that, upon what grounds he does it: my care shall be that I may never be found either doing or speaking anything that doth truly deserve contempt. Will any hate me? let him look to that. I for my part will be kind and loving unto all, and even unto him that hates me, whom-soever he be, will I be ready to show his error, not by way of exprobation or ostentation of my patience, but ingenuously and meekly: such as was that famous Phocion, if so be that he did not dissemble. For it is inwardly that these things must be: that the Gods who look inwardly, and not upon the outward appearance, may behold a man truly free from all indignation and grief. For what hurt can it be unto thee whatsoever any man else doth, as long as thou mayest do that which is proper and suitable to thine own nature? Wilt not thou (a man wholly appointed to be both what, and as the common good shall require) accept of that which is now seasonable to the nature of the universe?

plain_english: People look down on each other, yet they try to please each other. While they compete for status and worldly success, they sell out their souls to impress others.
original_excerpt: They contemn one another, and yet they seek to please one another: and whilest they seek to surpass one another in worldly pomp and greatness, they most debase and prostitute themselves in their better part one to another.

plain_english: How fake and dishonest is someone who says, "I've decided to be honest and straightforward with you from now on." What are you talking about? Why do you need to announce this? Your actions will speak for themselves. It should be written on your forehead. As soon as you speak, your face should show what's in your heart. It's like when someone in love can instantly read their partner's feelings just by looking at them. That's how a truly good and simple person should be. They should be as obvious as someone with bad body odor — you can tell what they're like the moment they walk in the room, whether you want to or not. But fake simplicity is worthless. Nothing is more shameful than false friendship. You must avoid this at all costs. Real goodness, simplicity, and kindness can't be hidden. As I said, they show themselves in your eyes and on your face.
original_excerpt: How rotten and insincere is he, that saith, I am resolved to carry myself hereafter towards you with all ingenuity and simplicity. O man, what doest thou mean! what needs this profession of thine? the thing itself will show it. It ought to be written upon thy forehead. No sooner thy voice is heard, than thy countenance must be able to show what is in thy mind: even as he that is loved knows presently by the looks of his sweetheart what is in her mind. Such must he be for all the world, that is truly simple and good, as he whose arm-holes are offensive, that whosoever stands by, as soon as ever he comes near him, may as it were smell him whether he will or no. But the affectation of simplicity is nowise laudable. There is nothing more shameful than perfidious friendship. Above all things, that must be avoided. However true goodness, simplicity, and kindness cannot so be hidden, but that as we have already said in the very eyes and countenance they will show themselves.

plain_english: Living happily comes from an inner power of the soul. It happens when you feel indifferent toward things that don't really matter. To feel this way, you must look at all worldly things — both the parts and the whole. Remember that nothing outside you can force an opinion on you. Nothing can reach you directly. Things just sit there, still and quiet. But we create opinions about them and stamp them into ourselves. We have the power not to create these opinions. And if they sneak in and hide somewhere in our minds, we have the power to erase them.
original_excerpt: To live happily is an inward power of the soul, when she is affected with indifferency, towards those things that are by their nature indifferent. To be thus affected she must consider all worldly objects both divided and whole: remembering withal that no object can of itself beget any opinion in us, neither can come to us, but stands without still and quiet; but that we ourselves beget, and as it were print in ourselves opinions concerning them. Now it is in our power, not to print them; and if they creep in and lurk in some corner, it is in our power to wipe them off.

plain_english: Remember that this careful attention you give to things will only last for a while. Then your life will end. What could stop you from handling all these things well? If they align with nature, enjoy them and let them please you. But if they go against nature, look for what fits your own nature. Whether it brings you praise or not, pursue it as fast as you can. No one should be blamed for seeking their own good and happiness.
original_excerpt: Remembering moreover, that this care and circumspection of thine, is to continue but for a while, and then thy life will be at an end. And what should hinder, but that thou mayest do well with all these things? For if they be according to nature, rejoice in them, and let them be pleasing and acceptable unto thee. But if they be against nature, seek thou that which is according to thine own nature, and whether it be for thy credit or no, use all possible speed for the attainment of it: for no man ought to be blamed, for seeking his own good and happiness.

plain_english: For everything you encounter, think about where it came from, what it's made of, and what it will become. Consider what it will be like after it changes. Remember that nothing is truly harmed by this process of change.
original_excerpt: Of everything thou must consider from whence it came, of what things it doth consist, and into what it will be changed: what will be the nature of it, or what it will be like unto when it is changed; and that it can suffer no hurt by this change.

plain_english: When other people act foolishly or badly, don't let it upset you. First, ask yourself: what does this have to do with me? Remember that we are all born to help each other. Then think of it this way: just as a ram leads the flock and a bull leads the herd, I was born to guide others. Go even deeper than this: if the universe isn't just random atoms colliding — which would be absurd — then there must be some nature that governs everything. If that's true, then lesser things exist to serve better things, and all good things exist to serve each other.
original_excerpt: And as for other men's either foolishness or wickedness, that it may not trouble and grieve thee; first generally thus; What reference have I unto these? and that we are all born for one another's good: then more particularly after another consideration; as a ram is first in a flock of sheep, and a bull in a herd of cattle, so am I born to rule over them. Begin yet higher, even from this: if atoms be not the beginning of all things, than which to believe nothing can be more absurd, then must we needs grant that there is a nature, that doth govern the universe. If such a nature, then are all worse things made for the better's sake; and all better for one another's sake.

plain_english: Second, think about what these people are really like — at dinner, in bed, and everywhere else. Most of all, notice how their beliefs force them to act the way they do. And see the pride they take in their actions. Third, if they're doing the right thing, you have no reason to be upset. If they're doing wrong, they must be acting against their own will out of ignorance. As Plato said, no soul chooses to make mistakes. So no one does wrong on purpose — it's always against their will. That's why people get upset when you accuse them of being unfair, unreasonable, greedy, or harmful to others.
original_excerpt: Secondly, what manner of men they be, at board, and upon their beds, and so forth. But above all things, how they are forced by their opinions that they hold, to do what they do; and even those things that they do, with what pride and self-conceit they do them. Thirdly, that if they do these things rightly, thou hast no reason to be grieved. But if not rightly, it must needs be that they do them against their wills, and through mere ignorance. For as, according to Plato's opinion, no soul doth willingly err, so by consequent neither doth it anything otherwise than it ought, but against her will. Therefore are they grieved, whensoever they hear themselves charged, either of injustice, or unconscionableness, or covetousness, or in general, of any injurious kind of dealing towards their neighbours.

plain_english: Fourth, you do wrong things too. You are just like them. You might avoid certain sins, but you still have the urge to commit them. Fear, pride, or some other foolish reason holds you back. Fifth, you don't really know if they have sinned at all. Many things are done for good reasons that you can't see. You need to know a lot about someone before you can judge their actions fairly. Sixth, when you get angry or upset, you forget that life is short. Soon we will all be dead.
original_excerpt: Fourthly, that thou thyself doest transgress in many things, and art even such another as they are. And though perchance thou doest forbear the very act of some sins, yet hast thou in thyself an habitual disposition to them, but that either through fear, or vainglory, or some such other ambitious foolish respect, thou art restrained. Fifthly, that whether they have sinned or no, thou doest not understand perfectly. For many things are done by way of discreet policy; and generally a man must know many things first, before he be able truly and judiciously to judge of another man's action. Sixthly, that whensoever thou doest take on grievously, or makest great woe, little doest thou remember then that a man's life is but for a moment of time, and that within a while we shall all be in our graves.

plain_english: Seventh, what truly troubles us is not other people's wrongdoing itself. Their sins exist only in their own minds and consciences. What troubles us is our own judgments about their actions. Let go of your belief that their wrongdoing is terrible, and your anger will disappear. But how do you let go? By reasoning with yourself that their actions are not truly shameful to you. If you think shameful things are the worst evil, you will be forced by natural instinct to avoid all evil. This will drive you to commit injustice yourself — to become a thief or anything else that helps you get what you want in this world. Eighth, the fits of anger and grief that follow cause far more harm than the original things that made us angry or sad.
original_excerpt: Seventhly, that it is not the sins and transgressions themselves that trouble us properly; for they have their existence in their minds and understandings only, that commit them; but our own opinions concerning those sins. Remove then, and be content to part with that conceit of thine, that it is a grievous thing, and thou hast removed thine anger. But how should I remove it? How? reasoning with thyself that it is not shameful. For if that which is shameful, be not the only true evil that is, thou also wilt be driven whilest thou doest follow the common instinct of nature, to avoid that which is evil, to commit many unjust things, and to become a thief, and anything, that will make to the attainment of thy intended worldly ends. Eighthly, how many things may and do oftentimes follow upon such fits of anger and grief; far more grievous in themselves, than those very things which we are so grieved or angry for.

plain_english: Ninth, that gentleness cannot be defeated, if it is real and natural, not fake or put on for show. How can even the most fierce and hateful person you can imagine keep fighting against you, if you stay gentle and loving toward them? Even when they are about to hurt you, if you remain calm and patient, ready to teach them and show them a better way?
original_excerpt: Ninthly, that meekness is a thing unconquerable, if it be true and natural, and not affected or hypocritical. For how shall even the most fierce and malicious that thou shalt conceive, be able to hold on against thee, if thou shalt still continue meek and loving unto him; and that even at that time, when he is about to do thee wrong, thou shalt be well disposed, and in good temper, with all meekness to teach him, and to instruct him better?

plain_english: For example, you might say: "My son, we were not born to hurt each other. When you hurt others, you hurt yourself more than them." Show him clearly that this is true. Point out that bees don't harm each other, and neither do other creatures that live together naturally. But when you do this, don't mock him or lecture him. Be gentle. Don't be harsh with your words. And don't do it to show off to others who might be watching. Do it so that only he hears you, even if other people are around.
original_excerpt: As for example; My son, we were not born for this, to hurt and annoy one another; it will be thy hurt not mine, my son: and so to show him forcibly and fully, that it is so in very deed: and that neither bees do it one to another, nor any other creatures that are naturally sociable. But this thou must do, not scoffingly, not by way of exprobation, but tenderly without any harshness of words. Neither must thou do it by way of exercise, or ostentation, that they that are by and hear thee, may admire thee: but so always that nobody be privy to it, but himself alone: yea, though there be more present at the same time.

plain_english: These nine lessons are gifts from the Muses. Remember them well. Start being a real man while you're still alive. But be careful not to flatter people or get angry with them. Both are equally unkind and harmful. When you feel strong emotions, remember this: anger is not manly. Being gentle and calm shows more humanity and more true strength. Real strength comes from staying calm. Anger has no power at all. The closer you get to being unshaken, the more powerful you become. Grief comes from weakness, and so does anger. When you're angry or grieving, you've been wounded. You've given in to your feelings like a coward.
original_excerpt: These nine particular heads, as so many gifts from the Muses, see that thou remember well: and begin one day, whilest thou art yet alive, to be a man indeed. But on the other side thou must take heed, as much to flatter them, as to be angry with them: for both are equally uncharitable, and equally hurtful. And in thy passions, take it presently to thy consideration, that to be angry is not the part of a man, but that to be meek and gentle, as it savours of more humanity, so of more manhood. That in this, there is strength and nerves, or vigour and fortitude: whereof anger and indignation is altogether void. For the nearer everything is unto unpassionateness, the nearer it is unto power. And as grief doth proceed from weakness, so doth anger. For both, both he that is angry and that grieveth, have received a wound, and cowardly have as it were yielded themselves unto their affections.

plain_english: Here's a tenth lesson from Hercules, leader of the Muses: it's foolish to expect there to be no evil people in the world. That's impossible. But to accept that evil people exist while refusing to let any of them wrong you personally? That's unfair and tyrannical.
original_excerpt: If thou wilt have a tenth also, receive this tenth gift from Hercules the guide and leader of the Muses: that is a mad man's part, to look that there should be no wicked men in the world, because it is impossible. Now for a man to brook well enough, that there should be wicked men in the world, but not to endure that any should transgress against himself, is against all equity, and indeed tyrannical.

plain_english: There are four bad habits of mind you need to watch for. When you catch yourself in any of them, fix it right away. Say to yourself: This thought isn't needed. This is unkind. This makes me sound like someone else's puppet - which is foolish and wrong. For the fourth habit, be harsh with yourself. Don't let the divine part of you bow down to the lower part - your body and its crude desires.
original_excerpt: Four several dispositions or inclinations there be of the mind and understanding, which to be aware of, thou must carefully observe: and whensoever thou doest discover them, thou must rectify them, saying to thyself concerning every one of them, This imagination is not necessary; this is uncharitable: this thou shalt speak as another man's slave, or instrument; than which nothing can be more senseless and absurd: for the fourth, thou shalt sharply check and upbraid thyself; for that thou doest suffer that more divine part in thee, to become subject and obnoxious to that more ignoble part of thy body, and the gross lusts and concupiscences thereof.

plain_english: Whatever fire or air is in you naturally wants to rise up. But it submits to the order of the universe and stays here in your mixed body. Whatever earth or water is in you naturally wants to sink down. Yet it goes against its nature and rises up and holds its place. Even the basic elements obey the universe. They wait patiently wherever they are placed, even when it goes against their nature, until they get the signal to separate and return. Isn't it shameful then that only your reasoning part refuses to obey? It won't even stay in its proper place, though nothing is asked of it that goes against its nature — only what agrees with it.
original_excerpt: What portion soever, either of air or fire there be in thee, although by nature it tend upwards, submitting nevertheless to the ordinance of the universe, it abides here below in this mixed body. So whatsoever is in thee, either earthy, or humid, although by nature it tend downwards, yet is it against its nature both raised upwards, and standing, or consistent. So obedient are even the elements themselves to the universe, abiding patiently wheresoever (though against their nature) they are placed, until the sound as it were of their retreat, and separation. Is it not a grievous thing then, that thy reasonable part only should be disobedient, and should not endure to keep its place: yea though it be nothing enjoined that is contrary unto it, but that only which is according to its nature?

plain_english: When the mind acts badly, we can't say it's following its nature like fire rising upward. It's doing the opposite. When the mind turns to injustice, lack of self-control, sadness, or fear, it separates itself from its true nature. When the mind complains about what divine providence has allowed to happen, it abandons its proper place. The mind was meant for holiness and reverence — which means humbly accepting God and His plan in all things. It was also meant for justice. These duties come from our nature as social beings. Without them, we can't live happily with others. They are the foundation of all just actions.
original_excerpt: For we cannot say of it when it is disobedient, as we say of the fire, or air, that it tends upwards towards its proper element, for then goes it the quite contrary way. For the motion of the mind to any injustice, or incontinency, or to sorrow, or to fear, is nothing else but a separation from nature. Also when the mind is grieved for anything that is happened by the divine providence, then doth it likewise forsake its own place. For it was ordained unto holiness and godliness, which specially consist in an humble submission to God and His providence in all things; as well as unto justice: these also being part of those duties, which as naturally sociable, we are bound unto; and without which we cannot happily converse one with another: yea and the very ground and fountain indeed of all just actions.

plain_english: A person who doesn't have the same main goal throughout life can't stay the same person. But it's not enough just to have a goal. You need to know what that goal should be. Most people think all kinds of things are good, but they disagree because their ideas have no solid ground. The only way to agree is to limit ourselves to what benefits everyone - to think nothing is good unless it's good for the community. So the goal we set for ourselves must also serve the common good. When someone directs all their private desires and plans toward that shared goal, all their actions will match up. This is how they stay the same person.
original_excerpt: He that hath not one and the self-same general end always as long as he liveth, cannot possibly be one and the self-same man always. But this will not suffice except thou add also what ought to be this general end. For as the general conceit and apprehension of all those things which upon no certain ground are by the greater part of men deemed good, cannot be uniform and agreeable, but that only which is limited and restrained by some certain proprieties and conditions, as of community: that nothing be conceived good, which is not commonly and publicly good: so must the end also that we propose unto ourselves, be common and sociable. For he that doth direct all his own private motions and purposes to that end, all his actions will be agreeable and uniform; and by that means will be still the same man.

plain_english: Remember the fable of the country mouse and the city mouse, and the great fear and terror the country mouse felt.
original_excerpt: Remember the fable of the country mouse and the city mouse, and the great fright and terror that this was put into.

plain_english: Socrates used to call the common beliefs and opinions of people the world's bugbears — things that scare silly children.
original_excerpt: Socrates was wont to call the common conceits and opinions of men, the common bugbears of the world: the proper terror of silly children.

plain_english: The Spartans would give their guests the shaded seats at public events. They were happy to sit anywhere themselves.
original_excerpt: The Lacedæmonians at their public spectacles were wont to appoint seats and forms for their strangers in the shadow, they themselves were content to sit anywhere.

plain_english: Socrates was asked by Perdiccas why he wouldn't come to him. Socrates said: "So I don't die the worst kind of death — unable to repay the kindness shown to me."
original_excerpt: What Socrates answered unto Perdiccas, why he did not come unto him, Lest of all deaths I should die the worst kind of death, said he: that is, not able to requite the good that hath been done unto me.

plain_english: In the ancient mystical writings of the Ephesians, there was a teaching that a person should always keep in mind one of the great figures from the past.
original_excerpt: In the ancient mystical letters of the Ephesians, there was an item, that a man should always have in his mind some one or other of the ancient worthies.

plain_english: The Pythagoreans had a morning habit. The first thing they did was look up at the sky. This reminded them of the stars and planets that always do their work without fail. It also reminded them of order, purity, and simple truth. No star hides behind a cover.
original_excerpt: The Pythagoreans were wont betimes in the morning the first thing they did, to look up unto the heavens, to put themselves in mind of them who constantly and invariably did perform their task: as also to put themselves in mind of orderliness, or good order, and of purity, and of naked simplicity. For no star or planet hath any cover before it.

plain_english: Think about how Socrates looked when he had to wrap himself in an animal skin because his wife Xanthippe had taken his clothes and left the house with them. Think about what he said to his friends who felt embarrassed for him and started to leave when they saw him dressed this way.
original_excerpt: How Socrates looked, when he was fain to gird himself with a skin, Xanthippe his wife having taken away his clothes, and carried them abroad with her, and what he said to his fellows and friends, who were ashamed; and out of respect to him, did retire themselves when they saw him thus decked.

plain_english: You have to be taught before you can write or read. It's even more true for how to live. You are born a slave to your senses and animal impulses. Without teaching, you have no real knowledge or sound judgment.
original_excerpt: In matter of writing or reading thou must needs be taught before thou can do either: much more in matter of life. 'For thou art born a mere slave, to thy senses and brutish affections;' destitute without teaching of all true knowledge and sound reason.

plain_english: 'My heart smiled within me.' 'They will attack even virtue itself with hateful and shameful words.'
original_excerpt: 'My heart smiled within me.' 'They will accuse even virtue herself; with heinous and opprobrious words.'

plain_english: People who want figs in winter when they can't get them are like people who desperately want children before they have them.
original_excerpt: As they that long after figs in winter when they cannot be had; so are they that long after children, before they be granted them.

plain_english: Epictetus said that whenever a father kisses his child, he should quietly think to himself: 'Perhaps tomorrow this child will die.' But people say these words are unlucky. No words are unlucky, he said, if they describe something natural. Really, it's no more unlucky than saying 'cut down grapes when they're ripe.'
original_excerpt: 'As often as a father kisseth his child, he should say secretly with himself' (said Epictetus,) 'tomorrow perchance shall he die.' But these words be ominous. No words ominous (said he) that signify anything that is natural: in very truth and deed not more ominous than this, 'to cut down grapes when they are ripe.'

plain_english: Green grapes, ripe grapes, dried grapes, raisins — so many changes of one thing. It doesn't turn into nothing. Instead, it changes into something that doesn't exist yet.
original_excerpt: Green grapes, ripe grapes, dried grapes, or raisins: so many changes and mutations of one thing, not into that which was not absolutely, but rather so many several changes and mutations, not into that which hath no being at all, but into that which is not yet in being.

plain_english: No one can steal your free will — this comes from Epictetus. He also taught that we should learn the skill of choosing what to believe. We should always watch our thoughts carefully. Make sure they stay measured and reserved, always kind, and focused on what things are really worth.
original_excerpt: 'Of the free will there is no thief or robber:' out of Epictetus; Whose is this also: that we should find a certain art and method of assenting; and that we should always observe with great care and heed the inclinations of our minds, that they may always be with their due restraint and reservation, always charitable, and according to the true worth of every present object.

plain_english: We should avoid desperate wanting. We should only reject things that are completely under our control. Don't think our struggle is about small, everyday matters. The real fight is this: will we be crazy like everyone else, or will philosophy help us stay wise and calm?
original_excerpt: And as for earnest longing, that we should altogether avoid it: and to use averseness in those things only, that wholly depend of our own wills. It is not about ordinary petty matters, believe it, that all our strife and contention is, but whether, with the vulgar, we should be mad, or by the help of philosophy wise and sober, said he.

plain_english: Socrates said, 'What do you want? The souls of rational people, or irrational ones? Rational ones. But which kind? Those whose reason is healthy and whole? Or those whose reason is damaged and corrupt? Those whose reason is healthy and whole. Then why don't you work for such souls? Because we already have them. Then why do you fight and argue with each other?'
original_excerpt: Socrates said, 'What will you have? the souls of reasonable, or unreasonable creatures? Of reasonable. But what? Of those whose reason is sound and perfect? or of those whose reason is vitiated and corrupted? Of those whose reason is sound and perfect. Why then labour ye not for such? Because we have them already. What then do ye so strive and contend between you?'
